newsitem.title: FRANCE: French scientist calls Greenpeace eco-terrorists.
newsitem.headline: French scientist calls Greenpeace eco-terrorists.

text.p: A leading French scientist has resigned as head of a nuclear safety commission after attacking Greenpeace activists as "totalitarians" preparing the world for "a gigantic collective suicide", officials said on Wednesday.
Charles Souleau, leader of a government-appointed study commission on France's controversial La Hague nuclear reprocessing plant, had been accused by colleagues of misrepresenting data.

Souleau announced in June that his team found no link between waste discharged from the plant into the English Channel and a cluster of leukaemia cases in young people living within 35 km (20 miles) of the area, on France's Normandy coast.

But the Greenpeace environmental group found high radioactivity levels in waste spewing into the Channel, and in sediment on the sea bottom near the plant, which is run by state nuclear company Cogema.
French health officials said that with Souleau's departure, there would be new studies on possible health risks in the area.
Souleau gave no public explanation for his decision to quit.

But in a memorandum distributed recently to colleagues, he called environmentalists "totalitarians" who threatened personal liberty and accused scientists questioning the plant's safety of being under the thumb of the "anglophone lobby", which he said controlled scientific publications.
"The environmental apocalypse described by Greenpeace...takes on a religious aspect, in reality more that of a fundamentalist sect," Souleau wrote in the memo.
"In a way, this is the terrorism of the year 2000, the same force which drives ordinary citizens to suicide, guided by their gurus. They are preparing us for a gigantic collective suicide."
Pierre Barbey, a commission member, accused Souleau of misrepresenting data on radiation exposure levels at a June 27 public meeting with area residents.

Barbey, who resigned from the commission in protest after that meeting, said the data had been supplied by Cogema but Souleau had presented them as if they had been calculated independently by the panel.
A mainstay of France's powerful nuclear industry, La Hague reprocesses spent nuclear fuel, such as plutonium, from countries including Britain, Germany and Japan.
Waste products created in the reprocessing are spewed into the sea from an underwater discharge pipe or belched into the air from its chimneys.
Cogema has insisted the Greenpeace measurements were invalid because the samples were taken too close to the pipe.
But new Environment Minister Dominique Voynet last month indefinitely banned fishing and yachting in the zone, saying she would not wait for additional safety studies before acting.

Voynet, head of France's Greens party and a minister in the leftist government which took power in June, described the step as "precautionary" and said it had not yet been established that there was a danger to health.
